translations.text: The life and conduct of our holy and honored father Apa Pisenthius, the bishop and hermit
of the mountain of Tsenti, as recorded by John the priest, for the day of his holy commemoration, which is the thirteenth of the month of Epip. In the peace of God. Amen.
The theme of this feast is full of joy on the day of our holy, Christ-bearing father Apa Pisenthius,
who is full of light, spreading a sweet fragrance at all times, not only by day but also by night.
All the animals of the earth and the birds of the sky rejoice, leaping and celebrating on the day of his honored, blessed departure,
which reached them, as the account will explain to us as we proceed.
I swore to remain silent and not speak of your achievements, because you have fled from human glory ever since you first became a monk, before you became a bishop.
And indeed, if we all gather together, each one has a prophecy, another has knowledge,
another has discernment, and another has a revelation, so that all may be built up.
But the holy apostle James declares in his general letter: “Whoever knows how to do good and does not do it, for him it is a sin.”
Let us understand whom the sacred apostle is speaking about when he says: “I know a man in Christ who, fourteen years ago—
whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up to the third heaven.
And I know that this man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up into paradise and heard secret words,
which a human being is not permitted to speak.”
Who, then, is the apostle speaking about, if not himself?
For all the saints flee from the glory of this world. Such, too, is the way of our honored father Apa Pisenthius, whom God has revealed to us in our own days,
as one who gives light to the whole world,
and as salt, strengthening everyone, according to what is written in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth.
But if the salt loses its flavor, what will it be salted with?”
And again: “You are the light of the world.”
He hides his ways of life, but God reveals them in every generation to those who do his will and keep his commandments, as it is written:
“The Lord is near to everyone who calls upon him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of everyone who fears him, and he will hear their plea and save them.”
Do you, then, wish to understand that he hates empty glory, and that he does not want anyone to go to destruction, or to recognize him through the practices he carries out?
Then listen attentively.
One day, while he was still a monk, before God called him to be a bishop, he was living alone in seclusion on the mountain of Tsenti.
His brother came to visit him. He was traveling with a faithful brother. They met the holy ascetic and received a blessing from his holy hands.
He asked them, “Do you have business in these parts?”
They answered, “First of all, we set out to come to you, visit you, and receive your blessing,
for worldly affairs have left us no time even to visit you for many days.
Besides that, we have a little business in this district that we want to settle. But pray for us, our father, that God may go with us.
If God gives us the opportunity, we will return to you again, greet you, and receive your blessing before returning home, if it is God’s will.”
The holy man answered, “Go joyfully, but watch yourselves, my children. Do not sin.
For the world we live in is nothing, because it is temporary.
Watch yourselves, my children, in these villages.
Do not associate with an evil woman.
Do not take interest from the poor.
If anyone in these parts owes you anything, do not pressure him or harass him.
Instead, attend to the things of the soul, so that God may show you his mercy.”
They answered, “Pray for us, our father.”
They left him and set out on the road, glorifying God for the words of instruction he had entrusted to them.
The holy hermit himself, Apa Pisenthius, stood up and began reciting from the beginning of the book of Jeremiah the prophet.
His brother went on his way with the faithful man who was traveling with him.
They settled their business in accordance with the word of the holy man, who had prayed to the Lord for them.
He made their journey go smoothly, and they returned to him [?] in haste, as before.
When they came to him, they heard him reciting the words of Saint Jeremiah with great calm and attentiveness.
They sat outside his dwelling for a little while, saying, “It is not right, and it is
not fitting for us to call in to the holy man until he has finished reciting and praying.”
When he had finished the prophet and completed the book, they stood up to knock at the door. But he began the prophet Ezekiel.
They sat down again and did not call in.
Finally, he finished the whole book of the prophet and fell silent, for evening had come.
When they knocked at the door, he answered them, “Bless me.”
He looked out at them in great astonishment and said to them, “How long have you been here?”
They said, “We came early, but we did not dare call in to you until you had finished meditating.”
Immediately he wept and beat his breast. He said to them, “I have suffered a great loss today, and all the hard work I have done has been for nothing.”
The holy man said these things because he was fleeing from the empty praise of people.
He was distressed that they had found out at all that he had been meditating.
Have you understood, then, my beloved, that the holy ones desire only the glory of God?
If not, listen to the holy psalmist David saying, “I have longed for your commandments.
Look upon me and have mercy on me.”
Paul, the wise man of our own day, also cries out, saying, “For in this we groan, longing to put on our dwelling from heaven.”
And again, “We have a building from God, an eternal house in the heavens, not made by human hands.”
Listen also to this great miracle that happened through him while he was still a monk, living quietly in his cell, before he became a bishop.
Once, on the third day of the Feast of Release, he became ill with a disease of the spleen.
He did not tell any of the brothers that he was ill, for he had said to them, “Pray for me,
so that I may go to Apa Abraham’s monastery and visit this brother who is there,
and, if the Lord allows me, return to you.”
He said this because he did not want anyone at all to know that he was ill.
But if anyone inquires carefully, “Why did this holy man say this?”
let him read the book of blessed Job. He will find the Lord saying to him, “Do you think I did these things to you for some other reason? Rather, it was so that you might be shown to be righteous.”
Paul also says, “I do all these things for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in it.”
When the holy Apa Pisenthius had been ill for a week, the brothers had not looked for him, thinking that he was in the cave.
They said to one another, “Young Pisenthius has been away a long time. Let us look for him.
Perhaps he became ill on the road, or perhaps exhaustion has brought him low and he has been unable to get up.”
They sent a brother to his priest to inquire about him.
When he went, by God’s providence, we saw the wonders of God.
Throughout all the days he spent lying sick, the saints attended to him, until the day the brother came to him.
When the brother came to him, he found the door of the little room he was in open.
By an opportunity provided by God, when he pulled the door latch, he called inside according to the brothers’ rule, saying, “Bless me.”
For on that day, [?], Saint Apa Elijah the Tishbite, of Mount Carmel, was beside him,
visiting him, for he had been sent by God to comfort him with his words.
When the brother had spent a long time standing and calling inside, “Bless me,”
the prophet rose to leave. Apa Pisentius took hold of him, saying,
“I will not let you go until I have taken comfort a little longer.”
The brother, for his part, when he received no answer, went straight inside without having himself announced at all.
He found the two holy men sitting there.
Apa Pisentius was lying down, while Saint Elijah was sitting beside him, visiting him.
When the brother went inside, he received a blessing from both of them.
He stood there, but he could not look into the face of the prophet Elijah because of the rays of light flashing in his face like lightning,
as it is written: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”
Saint Apa Pisentius became indignant with the brother.
He said to him, “Is this the brothers’ rule, that you should come inside without knocking?
If this had been a ruler, would you have been able to go in to him without being announced to him?”
The brother answered, “Forgive me, my father. I have sinned. I waited at the door, calling for a long time.
I thought that perhaps you were sick and unable to get up. That is why I came inside to see how you were.”
The prophet answered, “This is God’s arrangement.
He certainly deserves our greeting because of his good deeds. God has not deprived him of it.”
When the prophet had said these things, he left.
After he left, the brother said to Apa Pisentius, “Where is this bald brother from, that such great grace
surrounds him like this? Truly, I have never seen anyone like him, so joyful and full of every kind of light.
And I tell you, my brother, the moment I took his hands and kissed them, great strength came into my body.
I was no longer weak; I truly became strong. I rejoiced like someone who had [?] in a drinking place.”
If I say, “He is from this mountain,” I have never seen anyone in our province who resembles him, nor have I ever seen anyone with hair growing like his.
He said to the brother, “I will tell you, too, but you must keep this matter secret and not disclose it.”
The brother answered, “Might I not disclose it if, after some time, necessity overtakes me?”
“Why did you say that?
Have you not heard the angel Raphael speaking with Saint Tobit, saying,
‘It is good to conceal a king’s secret, but it is good to reveal the works of God’?
But I know that you hate the empty praise of people.
Tell me the whole truth about who this man is, and I will not trouble you.”
The thirteenth apostle, Apa Pisenthius, answered and said to the brother, “When I left you to go to the brother in Apa Abraham’s monastery and visit him,
I found that my body was weak.
I said, ‘Perhaps a fainting spell will overtake me on the road.’
My spleen made me ill from the time I withdrew from you, and I saw no one until you came to me.
When my spleen continued to torment me severely, I pleaded with the Lord about it, asking him to grant me healing.
When he saw my weakness and that I had no one with me, he sent one of the saints to me, and he granted healing to my body.
And I tell you that this man from whom you received a blessing is Elijah the Tishbite, the man of Mount Carmel,
who was taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire and a whirlwind.
I beg you, my God-loving brother, do not reveal this secret to anyone until the day of my visitation, so that you do not grieve me.”
When the brother heard these things, he was filled with great joy and comfort. He did not reveal the secret to anyone until the day when the God-loving clergy

of the Christ-loving city of Coptos took hold of the man who was truly worthy of the office of bishop, to take him to the holy patriarch Apa Damian, the archbishop, so that he might ordain him bishop.
So you have understood, my beloved, that Christ loves anyone who keeps the commandments of the monastic life and fulfills them without questioning.
He not only sends his saints to him, but they also see God, according to the vision granted to each one and in the form in which he wishes to reveal himself to them.
If not, listen to the God-breathed Scriptures. They will enlighten you fully, as is fitting and in accordance with the statements we have made
about our lord and father, the bishop Apa Pisenthius,
whom God revealed in our times as a source of strength not only for our district but for the entire land of orthodox Christians.
Come into the first book, Genesis, and let us see how it speaks about seeing God.
As for Jacob the patriarch, when Rebekah heard the words of Esau, her older son, who was angry with Jacob because of the blessing Isaac had given him, she called Jacob and said to him,
"Look, your brother is threatening you because of the blessing that Isaac, your father, gave you.
So now get up and go to Mesopotamia in Syria, to my brother Laban, and stay with him until your brother's furious anger
turns away from you, so that I do not lose both of you, my children, together in a single day."
Isaac also gave him instructions, and he went out. Jacob set out on the road. He said, "Go up to Mesopotamia."
He came upon a place and lay down to sleep, for the sun had set.
He put a stone under his head and slept, and he had a dream that night.
He saw a ladder firmly planted on the ground, with its top reaching up to heaven.
God's angels were going up and coming down on it.
The Lord stood firmly above it, and he appeared to him that night and spoke with him.
And when he had gone to Mesopotamia in Syria, God again spoke with him at night: "Lift your eyes and look with your own eyes at the white male goats and rams
mounting the sheep and goats, which give birth to offspring of various colors, ash-colored and speckled."
God also said to him in a vision at night, "I am the God of Isaac. Do not be afraid.
Be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth and rule over it."
And after he had blessed him with gold, silver, sheep, goats, and all his livestock,
he spoke with him again, saying, "Return to your home, and I will be with you."
So Jacob returned with his two wives, Leah and Rachel, their children, and their livestock.
When he reached the river to cross it, according to the words of holy Genesis, which the holy writer Moses wrote,
he said, "A man met him and wrestled with him until dawn."
When dawn came, Jacob said to him, "Tell me your name."
He said to him, "Why do you ask about my name?"
“It is wonderful.”
And he said to him, "Let me go, for daylight has come."
He said to him, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."
And he said to him, "What is your name?"
He said to him, "My name is Jacob."
He said to him, “You will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel will be your name, because you have prevailed with God and are powerful among men.”
He touched the joint of Jacob’s thigh, and his thigh became numb.
And he said, “I have seen God face to face,
and my soul has been saved.” The sun rose over him when the likeness of God withdrew.
As for us too, my beloved, it is fitting for us—
if God considered him worthy, came down into the world, and spoke with his creature about establishing
the salvation of their souls, how much more will he send his saints and comfort them in their sufferings?
Therefore, let no one disbelieve this statement that I have made about the holy Apa Pisentius, the bishop: that he was found worthy to see Elijah the Tishbite.
Otherwise, the written saying may be fulfilled concerning him: “God has closed the hearts of the unbelievers of this age, so that they will not see the light of the gospel of Christ.”
And again: “Do not walk with unbelievers.” And again: “The unbeliever does not have a single obol.”
Our Lord himself and our God, and our Lord and our Savior, cries out in the holy Gospels with his divine mouth concerning the man who brought his son to him,
who had an evil spirit, when he asked his father,
“How long has this afflicted him?”
He said, “Since his childhood. It often throws him into the water and into the fire to kill him.
But help us in whatever you can do, and have compassion on us.”
Jesus said to him, “Everything is possible for the one who believes.”
The child’s father cried out, “I believe! Help my unbelief!”
He rebuked the evil spirit and immediately cast it out of him because of the way his father believed.
Again, through the power of faith, a woman approached him who had been bleeding for twelve years and whom no one had been able to heal.
She merely touched the hem of his garment, and immediately her bleeding stopped.
He spoke to her, saying, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”
He also said to the disciples, “If you have faith
the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.”
And again: “You will say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you.”
It was also said about the holy Apa Pisentius himself: “It happened when he was young.”
While he was tending his father's sheep, God opened his eyes, and he saw a pillar of fire before him.
There were also some other young children tending the sheep with him.
He said to the young children tending the sheep with him, “Have you seen this pillar of fire before us?”
They said to him, “We have not seen it.”
He cried out toward heaven, saying, “God, open the eyes of these young children so that they too may see this pillar of fire, just as I have seen it.”
God heard his voice, and their eyes were opened, and they saw it.
You see, then, my beloved, that when God chose Moses, he spoke with him from his childhood, out of a pillar of fire, out of the bush.
As for Apa Pisentius, God came to him from his childhood, choosing him like Samuel, whom his mother gave to the Lord's temple in accordance with her vow.
As David, the sacred psalmist, said, “Holy Moses and Aaron were among his priests, and Samuel among those who call on his name.
They cried out to the Lord, and he listened to them. He spoke with them from a pillar of cloud. They kept his testimonies and the commands he gave them.”
There was also a brother on the mountain of Tsente who was very ill. His body had wasted away because his illness had lasted so long.
One day he longed for a little fish, and he told the holy Apa Pisentius,
who was still a monk at that time and had not yet become a bishop, “I long for a little fish, but I have not found any.”
The holy Apa Pisentius answered, “God will certainly provide it for you today.
Cast your care on the Lord, and he will sustain you. The prophet said, ‘He will never allow the righteous to be shaken.’”
The holy Apa Pisentius himself took his jar to fill it with water, for it was the season of the flooding, the flooding of the water.
As the holy Apa Pisentius walked, he cried out to the Lord, “God, do not neglect this brother in his distress. Rather, if it is your will, grant him his request.
Do not leave him distressed, Lord.”
When he went out onto the embankment to draw water, there was a great flood, for God had visited the land that year. Apa Pisentius looked,
and he saw a large fish [?] in the water, wriggling.

Oh, this great miracle of God! Instead of the blessed Apa Pisentius having to go into the water and drag the fish to the bank, the water of the [?] and the water of the channels carried it along and brought it to that very spot.
He was still about to fill his jar with water, as he told us with his own mouth, bearing witness to us. So he took the fish and gave it to the brother, saying to him, “God has fulfilled your request.
The one who sent Daniel his meal does not hesitate.”
He said, “It is he who has also willingly provided the fish for you today, for he has not left you distressed over what you asked of him.”
Truly, the prophet spoke well when he said, “The Lord is near to everyone who calls on him in truth.”
And he will hear their plea and save them.
The Lord will watch over everyone who loves him.
When the children of Israel rose up against Moses and Aaron, they said to him, “What is this you have done to us?
You brought us up out of the land of Egypt,
where we sat beside the pots of meat and ate our fill of bread. Now give us bread and meat.
Otherwise, we will stone you.” And the whole assembly spoke of stoning them.
And Moses cried out to the Lord, saying, “Lord, where will I find meat for these people to eat?
In just a little while they will stone me.”
And the Lord said to Moses, “I have heard the grumbling of the children of Israel against you.
Now command the children of Israel, saying, ‘Prepare yourselves for tomorrow, and you will eat meat.’ It will not be for two days,
nor for three, nor for ten days, but for a whole month you will eat, until it comes out of your nostrils.”
And he brought quails from the sea, two cubits above the ground.
You have understood, then, my beloved, that the prayer of a righteous person is very powerful and effective, as it is written.
As for Moses, the lawgiver of the old covenant, as soon as he called on the Lord on behalf of the multitude, the Lord did as he wished.
And the lawgiver of the new covenant, Apa Pisenthius, in turn,
as soon as he pleaded with the Lord on behalf of the brother who was a monk, the Lord did not disappoint him.
Instead, he fulfilled his request, just as it is written in the Psalms: “May the Lord fulfill all your requests.”
Listen also to this other great miracle that took place through the holy Apa Pisenthius while he was a monk, before he became a bishop.
One day he went to the well from which the brothers drank, to fill his jar with water.
But when he went to the well, he forgot the rope and the bucket and did not take them with him.
When he stood at the well, he prayed to the Lord, according to the custom of the brothers.
And he said, “Lord, you know that I do not have the strength to return to the monastery again to get the rope.
So command this water to come up to me, so that I can fill my jar with water and serve you for the rest of my days.
For you commanded your apostle Peter, ‘Walk on the water.’”
When he finished the prayer, the water rose until it reached the mouth of the well, and he filled his jar with water.
And he said to the water, “It is the Lord who commands you: ‘You, down to your place!’”

While the water was still flowing downward, a shepherd tending his flock of sheep among the thorn trees hurried to the mouth of the well. He watched the water swirling round and round in the well until it went down to its place.
To whom shall I compare you, O blessed Apa Pisentius?
Truly, you are like Moses the lawgiver, who made the sea divide to either side, and the children of Israel walked through it as on dry land.
The water became a wall for them on either side, to their right and to their left.
He was the one who spoke to the rock, and it poured out streams of water.
You too, O holy one, your prayer rose to the vault of heaven. The scripture was fulfilled which says, “He spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and they were created.”
You became a visionary like the prophets and spiritually perceptive like the apostles. You became a faithful steward.
Because of this, you were found worthy of the assembly of the saints.
God entrusted you with a multitude of souls.
You preached the good news like Paul, and in your wisdom you proclaimed the orthodox faith.
And you raised your voice with your words like a herald, crying out in your wisdom like a trumpet.
Who can honor you as you deserve, O holy and righteous one?
For you know hidden things beforehand, before they happen.
You used to speak to laypeople in songs and parables, and you used to speak to monks through spiritual interpretations.
You used to speak to rulers in parables and mysteries.
You were never too ashamed before anyone to tell them the truth, as it is written: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed.”
You used to guide those who came to you; [?] all of them to become believers.
And you gathered everyone to yourself in the bond of your love.
You obeyed Christ’s commandment and built your house on the holy rock.
You bore fruit with patience and with a pure and good heart.
You contemplated the spiritual feast; because of this, you found rest at the holy supper.
You sought pastures and good grazing grounds. For this reason, too, you always cared for the poor.
You secured the benefits of devotion to God. Because of this, you became a helmsman on the sea of the holy mysteries, and a holy one like the three young men.
And you were a father to many poor people in our time, and a father to orphans in our days.
You used to [?] peace for those far away, O God-loving father Apa Pisenthius.
And you trained those near you in sound teaching.
You became a spiritual merchant; therefore you freely bestowed your good things on everyone with great joy.
You sought and found, O God-loving father Apa Pisenthius, true leader of the flock.
You knocked, and the door was opened for you. You asked, and God granted all your requests.
There was great prosperity in your time, and great stability came to the Christians.
The church enjoyed prosperity in your days and in your generation.
Your people rejoiced in your wisdom, and your children delighted in your holy mysteries.
The rulers longed for your words, and all the converts sought your mysteries.
You beheld the man whose name is the Rising Sun.
Therefore he filled you with the radiance of the Holy Spirit.
You completed the ark of the Holy Spirit to a measure of one cubit, like Noah.
You became a lamp shining throughout our whole region.
Righteousness and peace shone before you all your days.
In your days, too, the foundation became radiant through your prayers and those of the saints who lived in it, namely Apa Colluthus and Apa Paham, these great saints.
And now, by the grace of God, let us tell you another wonder that we heard from those whose entire hope is the truth.
A man from our region spoke to us about the saint Apa Pisenthius himself, saying, “One day I went and received a blessing from him.
When he came out from his presence, I met Saint Apa Paham. He said to me, ‘Did you receive a blessing from young Pisenthius?’
I said to him, ‘Yes, my father, but you are the saint.’
He answered me, ‘Young Pisenthius truly is a saint, and you have received a great blessing if you have met him. For it was at the beginning that he prayed and the well filled with water.’”
He told us, “One day we saw a fire blazing in his house, and we said to one another, ‘What could young Pisenthius be lighting a fire for at this hour?’
They climbed up and looked down at him from the wall. They saw him standing in prayer, with his hands stretched out toward heaven,
his ten fingers like ten fiery lamps shining very brightly.”
When God called him to this ordination to the priesthood, of which he was worthy, he went and hid himself because he loved quiet.
When the God-loving clergy sought him out to seat him on the throne of the high priesthood,
This is what he truly deserves. They searched for him and found him hiding in the region of Jeme.
When they seized him, he cried out, repeating the words of the great John, the archbishop of Constantinople: “Oh, the solitude
that I know, but in which they will not leave me!”
Then they brought the holy man and seated him upon the holy [?]; they seated him on the bishop’s throne.
He had not pursued honor; rather, honor had pursued him. Those who seized him testified to us: “He declared to us with his own mouth,
‘Were it not that I would be disobeying the one who sent me, even if you were to cut off my head
or throw me into the sea, I would not obey you and abandon the solitude that God loves.
Have you yourselves not heard what is written in the Psalms: “Be still, and know that I am God”?’”
They pondered this among themselves, saying, “Who, then, is the one giving him orders? Is it a human being?”
They consulted one another, saying, “Let us tell the matter to the holy Apa Colluthus, a great man. He will get him to disclose it, and he will not hide the matter from him.”
Then they went to the holy Apa Colluthus and said to him, “Our father, when we took our father Apa Pisentius
to ordain him as bishop, he would not agree to carry out the ministry to which he had been appointed.
We spent many days pursuing him until we found him in the region of Jeme.
When he took hold of him, he wanted to refuse his office.
Afterward he said, ‘Were it not that I would be disobeying the one who sent me, even if you were to cut off my head, I would not obey you.’
We therefore ask Your Holiness to speak with him one day and ask him privately, ‘Who sent you?’
For this is an extraordinary thing.”
The holy Apa Colluthus asked him, “The God-loving clergy said
that Your Holiness said, ‘Were it not that I would be disobeying the one who sent me—for it is not my wish to hold an office like this.’
Who, then, is he?” The holy Apa Pisentius answered, “Before the clergy came in to my humble self,
I dozed for a little while, and a voice came to me three times, saying, ‘Pisentius, Pisentius, Pisentius!
Look, the clergy of the church have come for you.
Do not refuse the office to which you have been appointed, that of the [?] apostles. Instead, get up and follow them.
Do not leave the church a widow.’
When I heard these things, the clergy called in to me.
I went out and followed them, placing all my concern upon Jesus, because nothing will happen without God.
You have understood, then, my beloved, that these words of the wise Paul are true: “No one takes this honor for himself, but is appointed by God,
just as Aaron was.” So too Christ did not glorify himself by becoming high priest,
but it was the one who said to him, “Today I have fathered you,” and again, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”
And in this way he sat upon the episcopal throne in perfection, God having bestowed grace upon his face,
like Joseph, whose face no one could dare to look into without being afraid, because of the fear of God that was with him.
For who can count the acts of mercy he performed for the poor? Not only for those of his own district, but he also welcomes those who come to him,
and gives them whatever they ask of him.
You also know that he began using the small gift he had previously been given to distribute alms in every city and village, as far south as Aswan.
Whatever is brought to him each year according to the canons of the apostles, he secretly sends to people who fear God in every city
and village, so that they may give it to the poor during the winter, when the poor lack bread. He does not forget any poor person, as you know.
After some time, while our holy father Apa Pisenthius was tending his flock with great care,
he sent a letter to all the people of the district of Coptos, urging them: “Stop committing these great and grievous sins, as we have been told,
lest God become angry with you and hand you over to the barbarians, and they oppress you.”
He also wrote in that letter: “Unless you repent quickly, God will bring that nation against you without delay.
And again, after that nation, if you are disciplined, he will not stop stirring up wrath against you through a nation
harsh in speech and shameless in its bearing, whose people will show no respect for either an old person or a child.
He will afflict you with sufferings, just like the plagues of Pharaoh long ago, until he throws them [?] into the sea and his memory is utterly destroyed.
So let repentance remain continually with you in your homes at all times. Let mercy be in your hearts, and let your fasting increase upon your lips at all times.
For mercy triumphs over judgment, according to the words of James, the wise apostle.
For indeed, the third angel in God’s greeting is the angel of the spirit.
For charity saves a person from death and does not let him enter the darkness.
And: “It is better to give alms than to store up gold.”
And: “Give alms from what you have.
Do not let your eye begrudge you when you perform an act of mercy and righteousness.”
And again: “A little given as charity in righteousness is better than giving much through injustice.”
And do not turn your face away from any poor person, and God will not turn his face away from you.
And again: “Do not be afraid to give charity out of the little you have,” as the holy man Tobit said.
Look at this rich man, Nineveh, who forgot poor Lazarus: what did this do for him amid his punishments? He spoke in reply, in anguish:
“My father Abraham, send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am suffering in this fire.” And what a rebuke he heard in return!
Abraham said to him, “My son, remember that you received your good things during your life, while Lazarus received bad things.
But now he is being comforted here, while you are being tormented.” You did not show mercy so that mercy might be shown to you. You had no compassion for the poor,
while you fattened yourself on geese and ducks and the other animals, eating your crops
from the earth all by yourself, insatiably and with your inhumanity, drinking filtered wine from bowls.
As for the poor person, you forget him and show him no mercy out of what you possess.
And if he has even the smallest amount, you unjustly deprive him of it.
If you will not give him anything from what is yours, at least spare him and protect his rights. Do not burden him with your oppression.
You know that you and the poor person were formed from the same clay.
Do not cause him grief, so that God will not cause you grief.
There will be a place of judgment, and each person will be judged according to what he has done, whether good or evil.
These are the things that the God-loving father Apa Pisentius repeatedly writes to all the people.
But how will we be able to adorn the eulogy of the saint, except with words from his own mouth?
Rather, let us appeal to him to supply us with suitable material to deliver this eulogy, according to the measure of our insignificance.
We are not capable of reaching the height of his virtues, O good ascetic!
He is also adorned with the virtues of the Holy Spirit, a man of righteous deeds and all the commandments that are full of life.
Truly, even if I were to become entirely a tongue, I would not be able to honor you in proportion to one ten-thousandth of your virtues.
And even the little that we have managed to deposit in the treasury—it is your grace that has prepared it for us.
For we know that you have no need of our feeble tongue to speak a few words of praise to you, because your citizenship is
in heaven, according to the words of the fragrant tongue of Paul: “But our citizenship is in heaven, the place from which we wait expectantly.”
But let us say a few things about the saint, to the glory of God.
When God brought the Persian nation against us because of our sins, Apa Pisentius went to the mountain of Jeme and hid there because of the Persians.
For they had not yet taken the city of Coptos at that time; it was only the beginning of their rule.
I, John, was traveling with him at that time, serving as his attendant.
I took some water containers and put them in the place where we were hiding, so that we would have them for our needs throughout the days we would spend in hiding.
Pay close attention to this account, so that you may marvel and give glory to God, who performs these great wonders through his saints.
It is like what God once did for the children of Israel through Moses, when he said to him, “Lift up your staff and strike the rock, and it will pour out water for the people to drink.”
The same thing happened here too.
When he went again to his hiding place, I too was traveling with him. We stayed in the place where we were hiding and spent many days there.
All the little water we had left ran out. I said to my father, “We have no more water.”
My father answered, “God will not abandon us, my son, but will provide everything we need.
For he said, ‘Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself.’
And again, when Elijah the Tishbite was in the wilderness, the ravens [?] bread to him early each morning and again in the evening.
Again, when he slept under the tree called Rathmen, he got up and found a loaf of bread at his head and a container of water.
The angel said to him, ‘Get up, eat bread, and drink water.’
Elijah ate the bread and drank the water, and he traveled on that road for forty days and forty nights.
He ate no bread and drank no water.
So the one who provided Elijah with spiritual food because he followed him with all his heart—
if he sees that our resolve and our heart are directed sincerely toward him, he will care for us too.
For he said through the holy psalmist David, ‘Cast your care on the Lord, and he will sustain you.’
For God knows what you need before you ask him, just as he said in the holy Gospel.”
After my father said these things to me, he walked away from me.
I threw myself on the ground and pulled the folded cloth over my chest as I lay stretched out, sleeping, burning terribly from the heat and thirst for water.
After my father had gone a great distance, very far from me, he returned to me with his eyes full of light like the lights of heaven.
He was completely refreshed, like someone who had bathed in a bathing place. He said to me, “John, I see that you are suffering from thirst. Go, fetch water and drink.”
I answered him, “My father, the water containers have been empty since the third hour yesterday, and there is no water at all in our dwelling places.”
My father would fast for three days at a time. Sometimes, too, if his body was free from illness, he would fast for the entire week.
Again he said to me, “John, why do you remain disobedient?
Go, fetch some water and drink, for I see that you are suffering terribly from thirst.”
He said to him again, “John, from what I can see, you have become terribly parched with thirst and have suffered under the gloom of thirst for water.”
I answered him, “I have fallen into distress. But this is the truth: when you went into the desert
and returned to me again, and I saw your face full of joy, shining with light like that of Moses the lawgiver, my condition
became settled, and I stopped being thirsty.”
He answered and said to me, “If you have suffered like this for two days, then how great are the afflictions upon those who are in the gloom
of Hades, with the sleepless worm, the outer darkness, and the river of fire that flows before the true judge, in which we shall be tested!
Truly, my son, it is a fearful and trembling thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
After saying this, he said, “I think there is water in the vessels. Or have you forgotten? Look, there is some in them.”
But I, wretched John, am not worthy to tell of that miracle which I saw with my own eyes, for I consider myself alone to be poor.
When I went to the place where the vessels were—I declare to you, my beloved, by the terror that we shall all face—
I found them filled with water up to their mouths. Their water was white like milk and snow, and sweet like the waters of Gihon, which is turbid.
I went and asked my father, “I found the vessels full of water. Where does it come from, my lord and father?”
He answered me, “Be quiet, my son. The one who provides food for the ravens, which neither sow nor reap,
nor gather into storehouses, is the one who has provided us with this water that we need.
For whoever places his cares upon Jesus, he will indeed care for him wherever he goes.”
Have you understood, then, my beloved, that wherever he goes, all his hope is in Jesus, as he remembers what is written
in Jeremiah the prophet: “Cursed is the one whose hope rests on a human being.
But blessed is the person who has trusted in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope.
He will be like a tree planted beside water, and its roots will not reach out over a stream.”
What shall I say, and what shall I leave out, among all the honorable virtues of this honored, righteous, and blessed man?
First I shall speak about his service, and also about the grace that God gave him and the abundant gift that he bestowed on him, from his beginning to his end.
To whom shall I compare you, O blessed man, Apa Pisentius?
I will compare you to Abel, who established the worship of God and the high priesthood of God, being the first to present his sacrifices and offerings.
Therefore I will call your holy fatherhood blessed, because you became a father to orphans.
And the widow’s mouth blessed you, O holy bishop Apa Pisenthius.
You became a father to the weak and a place of shelter for strangers.
You became food for the hungry and water for the thirsty.
You became clothing for those lying naked and a garment for those lying naked.
You entered paradise in your mind and ate from the tree of immortality.
You are wise in your silence and discerning in your speech.
For your name reached your kings of the inhabited world.
You became gifted in the wisdom of God and knowledgeable in the holy mystery.
You sought his kingdom and his righteousness first, and God graciously gave you all these things.
You entered the promised land in your mind. Therefore God gave you strength to overcome the hidden Canaanites.
You contemplated all the spiritual examples and understood all the parables of the Gospels. You paid attention to all their spiritual interpretations.
All the learned speakers of the earth marveled at your wisdom, and they were at a loss before your defenses in this age.
The scholars, too, marveled at your wisdom, and all the senators marveled at your mysteries.
For all who were distressed would run to you, and you would help them in your goodness.
You became a righteous man in our days and a model in our generation, O holy bishop Apa Pisenthius, the blessed hermit.
The rulers became lovers of the poor in your days.
And they honored your service to God.
You were noble toward those near you, and the Romans honored you.
You put an end to the place of the [?].
And you shut the mouths of the wild beasts. The [?] were at a loss, and the financial officials withdrew.
You overcame Amalek like Joshua son of Nun, and you overcome the Amorites like Israel.
You took up the full armor of God. Therefore you were able to extinguish every flaming arrow of the evil one, and you fought against the devil’s schemes.
You took hold of the shield of faith and shod your feet with readiness for the gospel of peace.
Your fame reached the kings of the inhabited world. You became wise before the rulers, like Saint Athanasius, and God strengthened you in the Scriptures.
In your mind you searched for the ages to come, and you pursued the hidden levels—the wisdom of God.
You became a contemplative like the holy Apa Pachomius, the father of the monastic community.
God granted great stability in your days, and he bestowed his peace on you in your generation.
God brought forth your righteousness like the light, and he made your judgments like the light at noon.
You kept God's commandment. Therefore your peace became like a river in full flow, and your righteousness like the vast deep.
Your abundant spirit will be like the morning star, and your offspring like the sand on the seashore, which cannot be counted or numbered.
In your goodness you prayed for the whole world, and you urged everyone to turn to God in repentance.
You taught the lawless the ways of God, and you turned the ungodly away from their ungodliness.
You raised up the sick through your holy prayers, and you appealed to God on behalf of those possessed by demons.
To whom shall I compare you, blessed father Apa Pesynthius, the holy bishop?
You proved faithful in our generation and righteous in our days.
You became a scribe in your sensory faculties and a shorthand writer in spiritual matters.
You became a chief physician, treating everyone with a good heart.
You grew tall like a palm tree in God's righteousness, and you spread out like a plane tree in God's wisdom.
Through your virtue you gave off a sweet fragrance like cinnamon. The fragrance of your counsel reached the kings of the inhabited world.
You became a [?] through Christ's gift, and all your wonders were recounted in the cities of the whole world.
You became a revealer of sacred mysteries like Moses, and a singer of sacred hymns like David.
For we have often heard your mysteries in your letters, and in your letters we have seen the stature of your holy writings and your great wisdom.
You grew wings like an eagle, and you were transformed through the power of devotion to God, like an eagle.
God opened the eyes of your soul and showed you the gates of immortality, as he did for the Samaritan woman.
Your mind stirred the meanings of Scripture like the pick of a lyre, and you sang hymns to him with a ten-stringed harp.
To whom shall I compare you, holy shepherd Apa Pesynthius, the faithful priest?
I will compare you to Noah, whose holy sacrifices God smelled. For you found that work is good, and your lamp does not go out throughout the night.
You made heavenly garments for yourself from linen and wool, and you planted a vineyard from the fruit of your hands.
You became righteous in serving God with all your heart and all your soul.
God gave you rain, as he did Elijah.
He made bitter things sweet through your ministry, as he did through Elisha.
The mountains became sweet in your days, and the hills brought forth dew in your generation.
For you were building your children upon the unshakable rock, Christ, and you were building an everlasting faith within them.
You became a source of rest for the Egyptians and of joy for foreigners.
You endured hardship in serving the poor and became a help to all who are afflicted.
You beheld the perfect spiritual sheep, and you rested among your children, like Jacob.
[?] Afterward, you were laid beside your fathers, like David.
You became wise like Solomon, and you inherited the blessing through God.
Therefore you encountered slippery paths. You completed the race, kept the faith, and received the crown of righteousness upon your head.
You left descendants for yourself in Zion, O Apa Pisenthius, and you gained a household for yourself in the heavenly Jerusalem.
You took up the sword of the Holy Spirit through every prayer and every supplication, because you overcame the rulers of this world's darkness.
You beheld the sun of righteousness, who has healing beneath his wings. Therefore the eyes of your soul were illuminated.
You built the house of God like Solomon, and you completed its courtyard like Zerubbabel.
You walked in the field of [?]. Therefore you found the treasure of the holy mystery.
You became innocent in your heart. Therefore God gave you the shining star of his knowledge.
You ate of the heavenly bread, and you rejoiced in the tree of immortality.
To whom, then, shall I compare you, O blessed man, great priest, Apa Pisenthius?
I will compare you to Jacob, whom God remembered in his hardships because of his purity, and to whom he gave your inheritance.
I will compare you to Joseph, to whom God gave the key of the kingdom.
I will compare you to Samuel, who [?] the gifts of the high priesthood.
I will compare you to Samuel, who became a priest, to whom God gave the promise of priesthood from his childhood, and also the gift of prophecy.
I will compare you to the sons of Jonadab, who kept their father's commandment.
I will compare you to the great apostle, Saint Peter, who held the rank of archbishop.
I will also compare you to Paul, who cared for all the churches.
I will compare you to Zechariah the high priest, whom God filled with the Holy Spirit.
For God gave you wisdom from his mouth, like Solomon the wise.
You contemplated creation like Moses. God abolished idol worship in your days, as in the days of Uzziah.
Who will come to you with a sorrowful heart and not return rejoicing?
O true comforter, according to the words of David the psalmist: “Your word gave me life; your word comforted me.”
Truly, you resemble Moses, whose face was glorified, and who was exalted when God spoke with him.
You too, O lawgiver, the appearance of your face was glorified through the power of God that is with you.
The one whom all the saints befriended because of his purity and chastity, from the time when he was first a monk, before he received the honor of being a bishop.
Who could ever look into your face without being afraid, O you whose eyes blaze like the morning star, which sends out flashes of light at all times?
O blessed is the womb that bore you!
So if I wish to recount all your achievements, I enlist scribes to help me, like Moses the legislator
and lawgiver, until your strength is revealed, O perfect saint, Apa Pisenthius.
For you resemble the holy hermits Apa Palamon, Apa Pachomius, Apa Petronius, Apa Horsiesius, and Apa Theodore.
You resemble Saint Basil and Gregory the Theologian.
Who is as worthy of the priestly throne as you?
But no one can fully comprehend your wonderful mighty deeds and recount them with ease. Rather, those that we have seen with our own eyes
and those that we have heard with our own ears, O lovers of the word—one of his mighty deeds is what we will recount now.
For you God-loving children know that when the days of Easter,
of the forty days, draw near, the holy archbishops of Alexandria send a proclamation south throughout all Egypt,
informing the bishops, the clergy, and all the orthodox people: “Prepare yourselves, for the days of Easter have drawn near,”
and on which day of which month they are to begin the holy forty days, and at what time they are to end the fast.
Now the patriarch Apa Damian, the archbishop of Alexandria, sent God-loving clergy south with his holy proclamation, distributing it city by city.
For it was Saint Apa Damian who had ordained Saint Apa Pisenthius as bishop of the city of Coptos.
When the God-loving clergy reached our holy father Apa Pisenthius, they received a blessing from his holy hands and sat down.
It happened to him that day, according to God’s decree, while prominent men were sitting beside him.
A man belonging to your district, a shepherd who tended his sheep, came in to see him that day to receive his blessing.
At an opportune moment provided by God, the shepherd went inside after finding the door open.
He bowed down at the feet of Apa Pisentius, while the patriarch’s clergy were beside him.
When he got up, he kissed his holy feet and approached his holy hands to receive a blessing. He looked up into his face, but Pisentius drew his hand away from him.
He did not give him his hand, but cried out, “Who let this transgressor into this place, this shameless fellow?
Get out of here, you unclean man, you whom God detests!
Come, John, throw him out yourself!”
So I, John his disciple, seized him and threw him out.
When I was a little way outside the door, I asked him, “What have you done today that the great man is angry with you

so intensely? Truly, he spent the whole day cheerful and happy until the moment you came in to see him. If you had not done something very wrong today, his anger would not have flared up against you so intensely,
even with the patriarch’s men sitting beside him.
Confess to me, for it is written, ‘Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be forgiven.’”
The shepherd answered, saying, “Why did I not die today when I got up from sleep?
While I was tending the flock today in this thorn thicket, a woman I knew happened to pass along the road.
In my foolishness I seized her and slept with her, thinking that the great man would not find out.
The Lord is witness to my soul that the moment he looked down, my own conscience stirred within me, telling me that he knew what I had done.
A great trembling came over my whole body, and I was about to fall on my face, but you seized me and took me outside the door.
Otherwise, I would already have fallen on my face.”
Now that shepherd had brought some cheeses in a basket.
He said to me, “Please take these few cheeses from me and distribute them to the people beside you. Since I have brought them, do not grieve me.”
I answered him, “I cannot accept them without the great man’s permission, lest he find out and become angry with me.”
He answered me, “I adjure you by God Almighty to take them from me and give them to the poor on my behalf.”
When I heard the awesome name of God, I was afraid and accepted them from him because of the oath in the Lord’s name.
I took them and put them on top of some other cheeses that had been brought to me that day.
I said to myself, “I will not let the great man find out about me at all.”
That evening, when everything had grown quiet, he got up to give [?] to the clergy.
He said to me, “If any cheeses were brought to you today, bring me some so that I can send them to the archbishop’s clergy.”
I took all the cheeses and put the shepherd’s on top of them.
When he looked at them, he said to me, “Bring me a platter here.”
And he told this riddle, saying, “A man in daylight, whose eyes are open, with no darkness clouding them,
covers his eyes day and night and walks like a blind man, even though his eyes have light.
Will not everyone who sees him rebuke him, saying, ‘Why did God give light to your eyes, yet you preferred the appearance of blind people, who walk in darkness all the time?’”
I confess to you that when my father had finished saying these things to me,
he took all the cheeses that the shepherd had given me.
He separated them and laid them out on the platter. He said to me, “These cheeses, I tell you, belong to the shepherd whom I had them throw out today.
When you threw him out, you took them from him.
Now see whom you resemble!
You resemble Gehazi, who served under Elisha and who called the man back and received from him the two talents and the two robes.
See, then, how Elisha cursed him, making Naaman’s leprosy cling to his body!
Now get up and take them to him, wherever you find him.
Indeed, even if it is midnight, you must not sleep in this place until you have given them to him.”
I said to him, “Forgive me, my father.
“When I threw him out, he put me under solemn oaths. I was afraid of the oath by the Lord, so I took them from him.”
He answered, saying, “Do not let the sinner’s oil anoint my head.
Paul himself, the tongue of sweet fragrance, says in his letter, writing to the Corinthians, ‘I wrote to you in the letter
not to associate with sexually immoral people,’ and again, ‘If such a person is sexually immoral, do not eat with him.’
And again, ‘God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.’
And again, ‘Let there be no sexually immoral person, defiled like Esau.’ And again, ‘The sexually immoral will not inherit the kingdom of heaven.’
Go now and give them to him. Perhaps we will be able to save his soul from the devil’s grasp, for he too is a poor man.”
So I went and gave them to him that evening, and I returned to my place as my holy father had instructed.
You have understood, then, that our righteous father Apa Pisenthius is a Spirit-bearer and a righteous man. If not, listen to this account and marvel.
Once again, one day, my lord and father sent me on an urgent errand to the district of Jeme.
Time passed, and night fell before I returned.
As I came along the road leading back, two hyenas rushed at me while I was riding the donkey. They rushed at the donkey as though they were going to tear it apart.
Indeed, their teeth almost reached my feet.
I cried out, saying, “Prayers of my father, help me escape the mouths of these wild beasts!”
Before the words had left my mouth, the wild beasts withdrew without harming me at all.
They behaved as though they were being pursued, judging by the way they ran and their great haste,
when they heard the name of the great man, Apa Pisenthius.
When I had traveled a little farther,
some wolves rushed at me.
They threw a great deal of dirt into the air, and a great cloud of dust rose over me.
I also let go of the animal I was riding.
I cried out again, “God, through the prayers of my holy father Apa Pisenthius, you are the one who rescued me from the mouths of the hyenas.
Rescue me again now from the mouths of these wolves!” Before the words had left my mouth, one of those wolves let out a loud cry.
They all withdrew through the prayers of my holy father Apa Pisenthius.
They all withdrew through the prayers of my holy father Apa Pisenthius.
I, for my part, went north to the mountain of Tsente, glorifying God for what had happened to me, because he had rescued me from the mouths of the savage beasts.
When I went north, I found the holy man meditating on the Minor Prophets.
I took the animal into the stable for the livestock.
My father looked down at me from the top of the tower.
He said to me, “John!” I answered him, “Bless me, my father.”
He said to me, “Did I not tell you that if it grows late, you should not come north until morning?
The wild beasts would almost have devoured you, had it not been for God’s mercy.”
You see, then, my beloved, that he knew about everything that happened. Wherever he might be, he knew about whatever happened.
But he concealed himself through his way of life. He did not want glory from human beings to come to him.
As the wise Paul said, “I do not seek glory from people, either from you or from others.”
If I wanted to tell you about all the deeds we saw performed by the blessed elder Apa Pisenthius, the account would become far too long.
But since Scripture writes to us, “It is good to reveal the works of God to everyone,”
I will tell you a few things out of many about the virtues of this perfect man. After that, we will bring the account to an end.
Now it happened again one day that a man came to him from the district of Coptos, accompanied by his son, who had reached the age to enter into honorable marriage.
The two went in together, bowed down, and bowed down at his feet.
The holy man said to the man, “Why have you not found a wife for your son?”
For that man was a native of Coptos.
The man answered, “He is a young boy, my father. He has not yet reached the proper age, and he is chaste.”
The holy man answered, “Your son has indeed committed sexual immorality, and if you let him, he will tell the truth.”
The man said, “If he has committed sexual immorality, look, I place him in your hands to do with him whatever you wish.”
The holy prophet answered, “When you enter your village, you will meet a woman in the first street of your village.
She is the daughter of so-and-so. The one inside her will testify to you that it was your son who slept with her.
But do not think at all that I have said this on my own authority. No, I was informed by trustworthy people.
But if you listen to me, you will take her as a wife for him, since he has dishonored her.
And indeed, I will not tolerate leaving him like this until he marries her.
For the law commands, ‘If a man sleeps with a young woman who has not been betrothed, and takes her by force, he must live with her, giving her the bride-price [?] the bride-price of virgins.
And he must remain with the woman he has dishonored, whether she is poor or rich.’
Now, then, the devil has caused your son to fall with this woman. Go and take her as a wife for him.
Do not let him sin, so that God calls you to account for the salvation of his soul.
For if you join him in honorable marriage and he falls into another sin, the blood of such a person will be on his own head alone.
Do not let him find an accusation against you yourself before the judgment seat of Christ,
saying, ‘My father did not find me a wife,’ so that all the liability for his sin falls on you because you instructed him negligently, as was indicated
in the holy Scriptures concerning Eli the priest: he instructed his sons negligently.”
The man answered, “I will observe everything you have told me.”
For whoever disobeys you will be disobeying Christ, because the words that come from your mouth are words of life.
The blessed man said, “May Christ be with you. Go in peace.”
He left his presence and did as he had instructed them, and their hearts were greatly comforted.
Another day, our holy father Apa Pisentius the bishop was passing through the villages, visiting his churches.

When he had finished visiting them and was about to return to the monastery, he passed along the road of [?] outside [?]. A farmer brought him a cow of his own for him to mark with the sign of the cross.
Look at the power of God!
When the holy man imprinted the sign on the cow, his fingers sank into her.
When she gave birth, they found the sign that the holy man had imprinted.
He had marked her on the outside, and the sign appeared on the young animal in the form of white wool, like snow.
For all those suffering from any illness over whom the holy man stretches out his hand and makes the sign of the cross recover immediately.
Come, then, you whose hearts are upright toward God and the holy man,
and beseech him with tears and acts of repentance, so that he may appeal to Christ to have mercy on us when we meet him. For it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
If any of you dares to question the statement, because I dared to say that the holy bishop Apa Pisentius is Christ’s friend,
let him now turn to the passage in the holy Gospel according to John and listen to God speaking through the mouth of his beloved, Saint John the Evangelist,
saying, “You are my friends if you do what I command you.”
And again, “I have called you my friends because I have made known to you everything I heard from my Father.”
And again, “You did not choose me, but I chose you,
and I appointed you so that your fruit might endure, living forever.”
So you understand, my beloved, that whoever does God’s will is his friend and his brother,
just as he said in the holy Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and my sister and my mother.”
One day they brought them a little boy who was possessed by a demon.
He begged him, saying, “Please make the sign of the cross over him, for it is an evil demon.”
The holy man asked his father, “How long has it been since this seized him?”
He said, “Seven years now. I ask for your prayers, my father.
It throws him to the ground and thrashes him about on it like a camel, and his eyes fill with foam.”
And many times we give up on him, thinking that it has killed him.
And he does not speak at all. Please be so kind as to help him, my father.
Then my father called me, John.
He said to me, “Go to the basin in the assembly hall and bring me a little water so that I can pour it over this little boy, for, as I see it, this demon is tormenting him terribly.”
So I went into the assembly hall according to the command of my good and blessed father, the priest, and the superior of the place went into the sanctuary.
He filled the small vessel with water for me, and I brought it to the holy man.
The holy man made the sign of the cross over the water with his finger, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
He gave the water to the boy’s father, saying to him, “Take your son and go to your house.
Give him some of this holy water to drink, which I have given you from the basin in the assembly hall, and believe in Christ, and he will heal him.”
My father did this so that he would not give him a drink himself with his own hands and have the demon come out immediately,
and have people boast about him, saying, “Apa Pisenthius cast the demon out of such-and-such a man’s son,” because he did not want to receive glory from people.
When the man took his son to go home—as the man himself told me with his own mouth after returning to us a few days later—he said, “While I was still walking with my son,
when I had gone some distance from you, the demon threw him down on the ground and immediately convulsed him.
It cried out from within him, ‘Pisenthius, are you going to cast me out of my dwelling through the sign made by your finger?’
Immediately the little boy was cleansed. I took him into my house with joy, and it never returned to him until the day of his death.”
A few days later, he went to the great man.
He bowed before him and took hold of his hand, saying, “I tell you, the little boy has been cleansed of the demon.”
His father declared, “I tell you, my father, at the very moment when I gave him some of the water that you, father, had given me to drink,
the merciful Christ granted healing to my son through your holy prayers.”
He answered, “Everything is possible for the one who believes. In particular, the water of the sanctuary heals everyone who believes.
And do not think that this gift of healing belongs to me. No, certainly not!
Rather, it is the power of God, which is present in his holy places for those who go to them with upright faith and a heart without unbelief.
As for me, my son, I am of very little account in matters like these.”
When he had said these things, the man left him, glorifying God and thanking my blessed father.
Again, one day, a spirit of jealousy rushed upon a man’s heart.
He became jealous of his wife.
The devil, who hates what is good and enviously seeks to harm human nature, planted suspicion in her husband's heart against a man, as though that man had slept with her.
But that woman was innocent of the accusation, and the man too was innocent of the defilement attributed to him concerning the woman, as the account will tell us when we go on.
The man threw his wife out because of the malice in his heart toward her.
His father and mother made every effort, but they could not persuade the man to live with her.
As Solomon the wise said, “Her husband's heart is full of jealousy.” Let us not prolong the account any further.
Eventually the report reached the ears of the clergy of his village, and they excluded him from communion in the holy mysteries.
The clergy informed my holy father about the matter.
My father sent for him, saying, “[?] trouble yourself, so that I may meet you for a necessary discussion.”
The man shouted throughout the village, going from place to place [?], saying, “I will not go to Pisenthius!”
“What business does Pisenthius have with me?”
For that man was from Coptos.
But when he continued shouting angrily,
for the sun had set that day,
God revealed what he had said to the prophet: “Leave judgment to me; I will repay,” says Christ.
A terrible illness came upon that man during the night.
He suffered torment inside his body and was vomiting. Crying out in a loud voice, he said, “Take me to my father, Apa Pisenthius! I tell you, these things have happened to me because of him!”
“My father, please help me, for I am facing death! And if you do not take me to him, I will find no relief.”
His father and mother gave up hope for him, thinking that he was going to die.
He said, “Let us do as he asks; perhaps he will live. Since he said, ‘Take me to Apa Pisenthius the bishop,’ surely, if we take him
to him, he will make the sign of the cross over him, and he will stop suffering.”
For this was at the beginning of my father's time as bishop.
They brought him up to the mountain to my father. They called inside, and I went out to them.
His father said to me, “John, if you have ever seen me before, please inform the great man.
For my son is in danger of dying, and I trust in God that if he makes the sign of the cross over my son, he will find relief at once.
And he asked me, ‘Take me to Apa Pisenthius, and I will recover, because I am being tormented on his account.’”
If I said anything to him in my lack of education, being ignorant—
His son also cried out to me, “John, please take my answer in to the great man, for the agony of death has overtaken me.
Look, you can see me in my distress!
Why did my mouth not close and I die before I spoke that day?
Go quickly and tell my good father, Apa Pisentius, about my suffering.
Help me! Do not leave me to die at your door!”
When I heard these things from the man and his son, I went inside and told my father about the man and his son.
He said to me, “Leave him alone until he has been thoroughly disciplined, for he is an undisciplined man.”
I answered him, “If we leave him a little longer, he will die.
Only a little breath remains in him, and, from what I saw of him, he had a [?] fainting spell.”
My father said to me, “Let him come in.”
When he came inside with his father, he threw himself at my father’s feet for a long time.
My father said to him, “Get up, you undisciplined man.”
The man cried out, “As Christ lives, even if I remain prostrate at your feet for three more days, I will not get up unless you place your foot on my head.”
My father took hold of the hair of his head
and raised him up. He said to him, “Get up! Look, Christ has granted you healing, provided that you obey me from now on.”
The man answered, “[?] the distress from which your prayers saved me! If I have another two years to live, I will never dare disobey you.”
My father answered him, “These things have overtaken you because you threw your wife out into the street.
As for the deed you suspected her of committing with the man, they are both innocent.
But I tell you, if you want to be assured in your heart about her and the man whom you suspected of wrongdoing because of her—
for, my son, people look only at outward appearances, but God looks at the heart—
when you return home, take your wife back into your house.
God will give you the opportunity to be with her.
And I think she is pregnant. She will bear you a son, and the report spread about her is not true.
But believe me: she is innocent.
But if she bears a daughter, do not remain with her; throw her out.
She was not innocent of the charge brought against her, but violated her marriage.
But if it is a boy that she bears, the accusation made against her is not true.”
But she was saved from what they had plotted against her.
But if you want to put her under oath, I will not stop you, for God’s law commanded as follows:
“If a man’s wife transgresses, and he neglects her, and someone sleeps with her, having sexual intercourse with her in secret, out of her husband’s sight,

and he does not find out about her, and she has not conceived, and no witnesses have stood against her, they shall bring her before the priest. He shall put her under oath and give her the water of the curse to drink.
If the accusation made against her is true, that water causes her body to waste away with leprosy.
But if they have falsely accused her, she will conceive a child.”
Now then, my son, if you are convinced—if not, put her under oath. I will not stop you.
The man answered, saying, “From the moment your fatherhood spoke to me, my heart was fully convinced, and I will never again stop obeying you.”
He received a blessing and left him.
He went home with his father, glorifying God and Saint Apa Pisenthius.
When he entered his house, he was united with his wife and fathered a son, in accordance with the word of the apostolic Apa Pisenthius.
The man named his son Pisenthius.
He remained with her from that day until the day of his death.
The saint performed three miracles intertwined with one another. They were these: the woman whom he saved from the false accusation they had devised against her;
the man whom he set free; and her husband’s heart, which he cleansed of the schemes of the one whose power rests upon the nape of his heart, namely Satan.
He brought the married couple together again.
Truly, your wondrous life is exceedingly great, O angel of the Lord of hosts!
For who could recount all the miracles that took place through you in your childhood, and those that took place during your life as a monk?
As for those that took place through your hands after you became a bishop, which you brought about without wanting anyone to know of them, no one can reach the end of them.
But do not let the soul of that blessed man find fault with me because I have spoken these few words of praise about him.
And I think we have gone beyond measure in uttering these few insignificant words.
But let us obey the apostle’s instruction, in which he commands us, saying:
“Give everyone what you owe them: taxes to the one owed taxes, customs duties to the one owed customs duties, fear to the one owed fear, and honor to the one owed honor.”
Truly, you deserve every honor and all glory, as David the psalmist said: “Bring honor and reverence to Christ; bring glory to his holy name.”
Listen also to this other great miracle, and give glory to Christ.
Once again, a man came to him and begged him, saying, “Please help me, my father in Christ.
I owe a man thirty-six gold coins, and they are pressing me to pay them.
I have not been able to find them to give to him.
And I have nothing except one son, my only child. They have taken him into custody
and put him in prison, intending to make him a slave.
I beg you, father, to have compassion on me.
If you can, give me a little money so that I can go and pay it and they will release my only son to me.”
This man was a soldier from a foreign country, living in the region of Mount Teilaj.
He had heard of my father’s reputation as a bishop who gave generously. He got up
and came to him with his wife, wanting to test whether he was a loving man or not.
He put his wife aboard the boat and brought her [?]. He hid thirty-six gold coins with her aboard the boat.
Perhaps he had shed someone’s blood and taken them.
He came to my father, wanting to test whether the things he had heard about him were true or not.
On the day he came to the holy bishop Apa Pisenthius, he found him inside the holy congregation at Tsenti, celebrating the communal liturgy.
For it was the feast day of the archbishop and patriarch Apa Severus, archbishop of Antioch.
He sat down to wait until he came out of the congregation, so that he could bow before him and tell him what I have already related.
When the great man heard, he said to the soldier through the interpreter, “Pisenthius’s place is no place for mockery.
Go and take the thirty-six gold coins from your wife, who is aboard the boat at the mooring place.
Look, there they are, tied up in a handkerchief in her possession—the coins you brought to test us with.
See what you will do with them, since you shed a man’s blood
and took them from him, saying, ‘I brought them to give as charity for the salvation of my soul.’
Truly I tell you, even if the whole world were given in alms on your behalf, you would find no mercy
unless your blood were shed just as you shed your neighbor’s blood, as it is written: ‘Whoever sheds a person’s blood, his own blood will be shed in return,
because human beings were made in the image of God.’”
When the man heard these things, he was utterly amazed, for he had thought that the matter would remain hidden from the new Elisha.
He does not understand that it is the same Spirit who speaks through the prophets and the apostles.
For this God hears these things.
He left him weeping and went home deeply distressed.
You have understood that I did not lie at the beginning of this eulogy when I said that the blessed Apa Pisenthius is himself a bearer of the Spirit.
For whenever anyone went to him, he would know what business had brought them to him as soon as he looked into their face.
But because he hated the empty praise of people, he hid his way of life from us, so that no one would discover its full extent.
It also happened at the time when he was fleeing from the Persians and staying in seclusion on the mountain of Jeme.
He went a little way away from us to pray.
When he had spent three or four hours walking, praying here and there,
and no one could have counted all the prayers he offered day and night.
He would pray four hundred times during the night.
He turned toward me and spoke to me, John.
He said to me, “Be on your guard, for I came across a great dragon on the mountain today.
It is not far from us, but I trust in God that he will not leave it near us.”
At first, when this happened, I looked into the distance, about a bowshot away.
I saw a great many birds and vultures perched on a rocky crag.
He called to me and said, “I think God has struck down the dragon.”
He spoke again and said, “Why do you not pay attention to the words of the Scriptures
and understand them, as the wise David said: ‘You have made the Most High your refuge. No evil will be able to approach you,
nor will any plague be able to approach your dwellings. You will step upon a snake and a basilisk,
and you will trample a lion and a dragon. Because he has trusted in me, I will rescue him. I will shelter him because he has known my name.
He will call out to me, and I will answer him.’”
Now it happened, when God wished to take him away to the dwelling place of those who rejoice,
the place from which pain, sorrow, and sighing have fled, the dwelling place of the prophets, the patriarchs, and the apostles,
for he is a patriarch like Abraham, and he is an apostle like the apostles.
He is an apostle and a prophet among the prophets, like Samuel and the one after him.
He is a faithful high priest, like Moses and Aaron and those after them.

When he reached his final illness, in which he would go to his rest, it was the month of Epip in the fifth year. He called me on the night of the eighth of Epip and said to him, “John, is anyone with you?”
I said, “There is no one except Moses and Elisha, the priests, who have come to visit you.”
My father called out, “Moses, Moses, Moses!”
“Put your life in good order.
You know how you have conducted yourself under my authority.
Take good care of my papers, because you will need them, and your [?] there.”
He turned again to Elisha the priest and said to him, “Elisha, take good care of the brothers and hold firmly to what I have entrusted to you.
Ring the bell at the proper time, so that the brothers may say their prayers according to the brothers’ [?], and their souls may benefit through you.”
Elisha answered, “My father, I am close to going to join all my fathers.
If you are going to die, it is better for me to die first, because if the pillar on which we are established falls, the desolation of the mountain of Tsenti is near.
Where will we find another person to shepherd us as you do, O my lord and holy father, if you too depart?
You have already steered your ship toward a good pasture.
You have prepared yourself and will not be troubled, according to the words of the joyful David: ‘I prepared myself and was not troubled.’
But we will be deprived of you and become orphans from this day onward.”
My father answered, “Indeed, five more days have been given to me, beginning at the third hour of the day.”
I answered him, “What has happened to you, that you have said these things?”
He said to me, “Before I spoke with you, a trance came over me. A man of light came and stood before me.
He said to me, ‘Pisenthius, Pisenthius, Pisenthius,’ three times.
‘Prepare yourself, because you have five more days in this world, and then you will come to me.’
When he had said these things to me, he departed. Now,
look, I am going to join all my fathers.”
When my father said these things to us, a great cry of weeping immediately arose among us, because we would lose such a good father, a comforter of those in sorrow, one who grants repentance.
I testify to you before the Lord that, when my father heard about the Persian, he kept none of the possessions belonging to the poor for himself.
Even the [?] beside his head—he had it taken apart and gave it as alms to the poor.
What he gave with his own hands, and what he instructed me to give, I gave, along with what he sent to the faithful.
They were distributed village by village, according to each person's need. No one can know their full amount,
except God alone, who will give him glory for them all.
I said to my holy, Christ-bearing father, Apa Pisentius, “Perhaps, my father,
you think that we will not return again, seeing that you have left no possessions stored away for us?”
My father answered, “We will return by God's will, my son. And everything we have given to the poor,
Christ will give back to us doubled.”
What shall I say, or what shall I recount of this righteous man's acts of courage?
But let us return to his burial.
